Elliptic integrals and Jacobi elliptic functions

Source: R/hyper.R
elliptic-functions.Rd

Complete and incomplete elliptic integrals in Legendre form, with the parameter m (\(m = k^2\)) as scipy.special takes it, and the Jacobi elliptic functions.

Usage

sc_ellipk(m)

sc_ellipkm1(p)

sc_ellipkinc(phi, m)

sc_ellipe(m)

sc_ellipeinc(phi, m)

sc_ellipj(u, m)

Arguments

m

Numeric vector of parameters.

p

Numeric vector, \(1 - m\).

phi

Numeric vector of amplitudes.

u

Numeric vector.

Value

A double vector; for sc_ellipj(), a list with sn, cn, dn and ph.

Details

  • sc_ellipk(), sc_ellipe(): complete integrals \(K(m)\), \(E(m)\).

  • sc_ellipkm1(): \(K(1 - p)\), accurate near \(m = 1\).

  • sc_ellipkinc(), sc_ellipeinc(): incomplete \(F(\phi | m)\) and \(E(\phi | m)\).

  • sc_ellipj(): \(sn\), \(cn\), \(dn\) and the amplitude \(\phi\), as a named list, as SciPy returns a tuple.

Arguments are recycled, NA gives NA, and results take their dimensions, or else their names, from the arguments as base R arithmetic does; see sc_seterr() for the conditions the kernels raise.

Windows

R on Windows is built with Rtools, whose C library (mingw-w64 v11) computes sin() and cos() with x87 argument reduction. Near a zero of the cosine it loses relative accuracy, and sc_ellipj(u, 0), which is cos(u) exactly, inherits that for u near pi / 2 on Windows only.

Other packages

In gsl: ellint_Kcomp(), ellint_Ecomp(), ellint_F() and ellint_E(), which take the modulus \(k\) where SciPy takes the parameter \(m = k^2\): sc_ellipk(m) is ellint_Kcomp(sqrt(m)). Its elljac(u, m) takes \(m\), as sc_ellipj() does.

See also

https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/special.html#elliptic-functions-and-integrals

Examples

sc_ellipk(c(0, 0.5, 0.9))
#> [1] 1.570796 1.854075 2.578092
sc_ellipkinc(pi / 4, 0.5)
#> [1] 0.8260179
sc_ellipj(1, 0.5)
#> $sn
#> [1] 0.8030018
#> 
#> $cn
#> [1] 0.5959766
#> 
#> $dn
#> [1] 0.823161
#> 
#> $ph
#> [1] 0.9323151
#>
